passages.text: A cantilever is a vital element in civil construction and structural engineering. It is a rigid structural member that extends horizontally and is supported only at one end. This design allows the free end to project beyond the support, carrying loads without additional bracing. If you’re wondering what is a cantilever, you’re about to discover how this simple concept powers some of the most iconic structures in the world. Cantilevers are widely used in bridges, buildings, balconies, and other construction applications where overhanging structures are needed. Their versatility and efficiency make them a favorite among architects and civil engineers alike. Types of Cantilevers Cantilevers come in various forms based on structural needs. Below are the major types: 1. Simple Cantilever A simple cantilever consists of a beam fixed at one end and free at the other. This type is common in balconies and overhanging roofs. 2. Continuous Cantilever This type is supported at more than one point but still extends beyond its final support. It offers more stability and can handle greater loads. 3. Published on 04 September, 2026 | Updated on 04 September, 2026 Introduction A cantilever is a structural element that projects beyond its primary support while being supported mainly at one end. Unlike a conventional beam that may have supports at both ends, a cantilever can create an open overhang without requiring a column directly underneath its projecting portion. This structural principle is widely used in modern architecture for balconies, roof extensions, canopies, floating staircases, viewing platforms, and dramatic building overhangs. Understanding how a cantilever works requires looking at its support condition, load path, bending moment, shear force, deflection, and connection design. What Is a Cantilever? A cantilever is typically fixed or rigidly connected at one end while the other end extends freely into space. When a load acts on the projecting portion, the load travels through the cantilever toward the fixed support. The support must resist both vertical forces and the bending moment generated by the overhang. This makes the connection and supporting structural system particularly important. passages.text: Cantilever A cantilever is a structural element that is firmly attached to a fixed structure at one end and is unsupported at the other end. Sometimes it projects from a vertical surface such as a wall. A cantilever can be in the form of a beam, plate, truss, or slab. When subjected to a structural load at its far, unsupported end, the cantilever carries the load to the support where it applies a shear stress and a bending moment.[1] Cantilever construction allows overhanging structures without external support. In bridges, railroad crossings, towers, and buildings [edit] Cantilevers are widely found in construction, notably in cantilever bridges and balconies (see corbel). In cantilever bridges, the cantilevers are usually built as pairs, with each cantilever used to support one end of a central section. The Forth Bridge in Scotland is an example of a cantilever truss bridge. A cantilever in a traditionally timber framed building is called a jetty or forebay. In the southern United States, a historic barn type is the cantilever barn of log construction. Temporary cantilevers are often used in construction. passages.text: A cantilever is a structural element, like a floor joist or beam, that extends beyond its support point without additional bearing beneath the extended portion, projecting outward and relying entirely on the strength of the structural member itself along with adequate anchoring at the supported end. This structural principle appears throughout residential construction, from a bay window projecting beyond a foundation wall to a small deck extension supported entirely by extended floor joists. Because a cantilevered structure has no support at its outer end, the load it can safely carry, and how far it can safely extend, is limited by the structural member’s strength and the quality of its anchoring at the supported end. passages.text: A cantilever is a beam that is supported at only one end and carries a load at the other end. Cantilevers are often used in architecture, as they allow for overhanging structures that do not need to be supported from the outside. In many cases, partially-constructed buildings create cantilevers that allow builders to work without needing falsework. Airplane wings are also cantilevers, as they are usually only supported from the body of the plane. Because only one end of the beam is supported, a cantilever is typically subjected to a great deal of stress. The top half of a cantilever experiences tensile stress, which elongates the fibers of the beam. The bottom half is subjected to compressive stress, which compresses the fibers. If it can't handle all of the stress, a cantilever may arc downward or even break. As such, engineers and architects work to design beams and balance loads in such a way that they will not suffer from such structural issues. Sometimes, cantilevers are used in the construction of bridges. Such a type of bridge is known as a cantilever bridge. The wings of most modern aircraft are cantilevers, as they are built into the body of the aircraft but are not supported on the end. Earlier aircraft were usually designed with two or more wings on each side that supported each other, like a truss on a bridge. Cantilever vs. Rafter Tail A cantilever describes the general structural principle of an unsupported extension carrying load. Conclusion A cantilever is a structural element supported primarily at one end and projecting beyond its support. Its ability to create open overhangs without columns underneath makes it especially useful in modern building design. The fundamental behavior is based on load transfer, bending, shear, stiffness, and connection capacity. As cantilever length increases, structural demands and deflection can increase significantly, making proper structural analysis essential. Whether used for a balcony, roof extension, canopy, staircase, or major architectural overhang, a cantilever must be designed as part of an integrated structural system. Its dimensions, loads, reinforcement, member sizes, connections, and stability requirements must be established through project-specific engineering design and applicable standards. Bending and Shear Near the Support The fixed support is generally the most highly stressed region of a typical cantilever. Bending moment and shear force are concentrated near this connection, making the support region critical for structural design. In reinforced-concrete cantilevers, the primary tension reinforcement for a typical downward loading condition is generally positioned near the top of the member and must be properly anchored into the supporting structure. Steel cantilevers similarly require adequate connection strength, member capacity, stability, and load transfer between the projecting steel element and its supporting frame or core. Deflection and Vibration Control Strength is not the only consideration in cantilever design. Deflection can become an important serviceability issue, particularly for long and slender projections. For a simplified cantilever with a point load at its free end, the elastic tip deflection can be expressed as: \[\delta=\frac{PL^3}{3EI}\] where \(E\) is the material's elastic modulus and \(I\) is the second moment of area. The \(L^3\) relationship demonstrates why cantilever length has a strong influence on deflection. A longer projection can become considerably more flexible even when its strength remains adequate.

For a simplified cantilever carrying a point load \(P\) at its free end, the maximum bending moment at the fixed support is: \[M_{\max}=PL\] where \(P\) is the applied load and \(L\) is the cantilever length. This equation demonstrates an important principle: as the cantilever becomes longer, the bending demand at the support increases. How Does a Cantilever Carry Loads? The load path of a cantilever begins at the applied load and continues through the projecting member toward the fixed connection. The support then transfers the resulting forces and moments into the rest of the structural system and ultimately toward the foundations. For a uniformly distributed load \(w\), the simplified maximum bending moment is: \[M_{\max}=\frac{wL^2}{2}\] This relationship shows why increasing cantilever length can have a significant effect on structural demand. Because the bending moment varies with the square of the length for a uniformly distributed load, even a moderate increase in projection can substantially increase the required structural capacity. Cantilevers in Modern Architecture Cantilevers have become an important architectural feature because they allow designers to create large open spaces and visually floating forms. A building may use a cantilevered balcony to extend beyond the facade, a roof canopy to provide shade, or a projecting upper floor to create additional usable space without adding columns below. This can be particularly valuable where unobstructed space is desired at ground level. Cantilever systems can also support architectural concepts involving floating staircases, dramatic roof forms, observation platforms, and modern residential extensions. However, an attractive cantilever is only successful when architectural intent and structural requirements are integrated from the beginning of the design process. Microcantilever [edit] Cantilevered beams are the most ubiquitous structures in the field of microelectromechanical systems (MEMS). An early example of a MEMS cantilever is the Resonistor,[7][8] an electromechanical monolithic resonator. MEMS cantilevers are commonly fabricated from silicon (Si), silicon nitride (Si3N4), or polymers. The fabrication process typically involves undercutting the cantilever structure to release it, often with an anisotropic wet or dry etching technique. Without cantilever transducers, atomic force microscopy would not be possible. A large number of research groups are attempting to develop cantilever arrays as biosensors for medical diagnostic applications. MEMS cantilevers are also finding application as radio frequency filters and resonators. Types of MEMS cantilevers include unimorphs and bimorphs.
